study_identification.author_journal_year: Pinaya et al., Human Brain Mapping, 2019
study_identification.title: Using deep autoencoders to identify abnormal brain structural patterns in neuropsychiatric disorders: A large-scale multi-sample study

study_characteristics.study_objective: To propose an alternative conceptual and practical approach for investigating brain-based disorders which aim to overcome the limitations of machine learning models that require a large number of cases and lack of interpretability. The authors used a deep autoencoder to create a normative model using structural magnetic resonance imaging data from healthy people and then used this model to estimate total and regional neuroanatomical deviation in individual patients with schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: The authors state that to avoid the effects of different sites, scanners, and populations, they restricted statistical comparisons to patient and control groups from the same data set. They also included age and sex as covariates in the model.

software_tool.answer: Tensorflow v.1.4; Keras v.2.1; Python; Scikit-learn v0.19.2

response_variable.answer: Cortical thickness (68 regions); Subcortical volumes (36 structures)

predictor_effects.answer: The paper states that age and sex were incorporated into the model, but does not specify whether they were treated as fixed or random effects. However, the description of the model suggests they were treated as fixed effects.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The authors address site effects by comparing patients and controls within the same dataset and include age and sex as predictors in their model. However, they do not explicitly model other potential nuisance variables like head motion or image quality.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To avoid the effects of different sites, scanners, and populations, we restricted statistical comparisons to patient and control groups from the same data set. ... we added information about our samples (in our case, age and sex values) in the structure of the model.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The model was trained and validated using a 10-fold cross-validation process on the HCP dataset.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: We executed a cross-validation process on the HCP data to determine the best number of neurons for the layers of our deep autoencoder. We obtained the best performance from the structure with the 104 -> 100 -> 75 -> 100 -> 104 configurations... with mean reconstruction error of 0.40 +/- 0.01

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The model was not validated on an independent dataset from the same domain (i.e., another healthy control dataset).

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The model was trained on the HCP dataset and then tested on two different clinical datasets (NUSDAST and ABIDE), which represent different domains.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: After training this model, we used it to encode and reconstruct the data from two public data sets with psychiatry patients. These data sets composed of patients with schizophrenia (SCZ) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD)

clinical_dataset.answer: Northwestern University Schizophrenia Data and Software Tool (NUSDAST); Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE)

clinical_groups_age.answer: SCZ: mean 25.5, sd 3.92, range 22-36; ASD: mean 27.3, sd 4.1, range 22-36

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: The authors used a two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test to verify whether the medians of deviation metric are significantly different between healthy controls and patients for each clinical group. They also used Cliff's delta to measure the magnitude of neuroanatomical deviations.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: The deep autoencoder was able to detect different patterns of neuroanatomical alteration between neuropsychiatric patients and healthy controls on the basis of their reconstruction error, and it was also able to detect distinct patterns of neuroanatomical deviations in SCZ and ASD.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The deep autoencoder yielded a mean deviation metric of 0.97 +/- 0.23 for the HC group and 1.14 +/- 0.28 for the SCZ group from the NUSDAST data set (Cliff's delta = 0.4142). The deep autoencoder was also applied to the ABIDE data set, obtaining a mean deviation metric of 1.09 +/- 0.30 for the HC group and 1.27 +/- 0.40 for the ASD group (Cliff's delta = 0.2764). The deviation metric was significantly higher for the SCZ groups than the corresponding HC groups (p = .001) and for the ASD group than the corresponding HC group (p < .001).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The authors list several limitations, including the high individual variability within each group, the fact that the model may not be capable of detecting all abnormalities in all brain-based disorders, the potential influence of head motion, the lack of manual correction of the preprocessing, and the inability to establish the direction of the alterations.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The deep autoencoder provides a flexible and promising framework which could be applied to different neuroimaging modalities (e.g., functional MRI) and different types of preprocessing (e.g., voxel-based morphometry) in future studies.
